doc.title: Louis Hayes interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000

title: Reactions to 'Work Song' and learning the music business
summary: Hayes found 'The Work Song' square and played it nightly; he learned that music is a business.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Did you have a feeling when you did some of the tunes like “The Work Song” and “Jive Samba,” that these were going to be hits? I’m not sure how you define a hit in the jazz world. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-
But did you go away with a feeling like man we’ve got something there?

No, I didn’t. And sometimes, I know myself, sometimes — I enjoyed the playing, good music, I always enjoy, especially when you’re playing with creative people like Cannon and Nat and Yusef and Charles Lloyd and Sam Jones. But sometimes I didn’t, I thought the stuff was kind of square, especially “The Work Song.”
You thought it was square, yeah.
You want me to go buh buh?
And this was something, you know, we had to play this every night, doggone it.
That’s great to hear. You just never know.

Yeah. Because I was much younger, and I wanted to be, you know I’ve tried my best to be as creative as possible, and some of those things I had to learn about business. Music is a business. And so I had to kind of start getting it together and learning about that because I was looking at it just for fun and being creative, and I wasn’t looking at things that way a lot of times at that time.
Yeah. I mean so that’s a learning experience in itself.
If you want to be successful sometimes, you can’t play exactly the way you had envisioned at certain times.
